# Ezra Chapter 4 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 469r–469v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EZR_004_page_001.jpg

---

**1** When the enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the returned exiles were building a temple to the LORD, the God of Israel, **2** they came to Zerubbabel and the family leaders and said, "Let us help you build! We worship your God too. We have been offering sacrifices to him ever since King Esarhaddon of Assyria brought us here."

**3** But Zerubbabel, Jeshua, and the other leaders of Israel answered them, "You have no part in building a house to our God. We alone will build it for the LORD, the God of Israel, just as King Cyrus of Persia commanded us."

**4** Then the local people set about discouraging and intimidating the people of Judah to keep them from building. **5** They bribed officials to work against the Jews and to frustrate their plans. This continued throughout the reign of King Cyrus of Persia and into the reign of King Darius.

**6** Later, at the beginning of the reign of King Xerxes, the enemies filed a formal accusation against the people of Judah and Jerusalem.

**7** And during the reign of King Artaxerxes of Persia, Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and their colleagues wrote a letter to the king. It was written in Aramaic script and translated.

**8** Rehum the commanding officer and Shimshai the court secretary composed a letter against Jerusalem and sent it to King Artaxerxes. **9** The letter was from Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates — the judges, governors, officials, and people from Persia, Erech, Babylon, and Susa (the Elamites), **10** as well as all the other peoples whom the great and honorable Ashurbanipal had deported and resettled in Samaria and the rest of the province west of the Euphrates.

**11** Here is a copy of their letter: "To King Artaxerxes, from your servants in the province west of the Euphrates. Greetings.

**12** The king should know that the Jews who came from you to us have gone to Jerusalem and are rebuilding that rebellious and wicked city. They are restoring the walls and repairing the foundations.

**13** The king should also know that if this city is rebuilt and its walls restored, the Jews will stop paying taxes, tribute, and duty, and the royal treasury will suffer. **14** Since we are loyal servants of the crown, we cannot stand by and watch the king be dishonored. Therefore we are sending this report **15** so that a search can be made in the royal archives. You will find in those records that this city has a long history of rebellion against kings and that it has been a center of revolt and sedition from ancient times. That is why it was destroyed. **16** We wish to inform the king that if this city is rebuilt and its walls completed, you will lose control of the entire province west of the Euphrates."

**17** The king sent this reply: "To Rehum the commander, Shimshai the secretary, and their associates living in Samaria and elsewhere in the province west of the Euphrates. Greetings.

**18** The letter you sent us has been read and translated in my presence. **19** I ordered an investigation, and it has indeed been found that this city has a long history of revolt against kings, with rebellion and sedition stirred up within it. **20** Powerful kings once ruled from Jerusalem over the entire region west of the Euphrates, and tribute, customs, and tolls were paid to them. **21** Therefore, issue an order for these men to stop their work. This city must not be rebuilt until I give further orders. **22** See that you do not neglect this matter. Why allow the damage to increase and threaten the king's interests?"

**23** As soon as the copy of King Artaxerxes' letter was read to Rehum, Shimshai, and their associates, they rushed to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop building.

**24** So the work on God's temple in Jerusalem came to a halt. It remained at a standstill until the second year of King Darius of Persia.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verses 1-3 — A dangerous offer:** The offer to "help build" was not innocent. These were peoples settled in the land by the Assyrians who practiced syncretistic worship — honoring YHWH alongside other gods (2 Kings 17:24-41). The Jewish leaders' refusal was not mere exclusivism but a theological boundary: the temple of YHWH could not be built on compromised foundations.

**Verses 12-16 — Weaponizing bureaucracy:** The opponents achieved through paperwork what they could not through intimidation. Their letter was masterfully crafted — they conflated temple construction (authorized by Cyrus) with wall-building (a military threat), appealed to the king's self-interest, and invoked historical precedent. It is a timeless portrait of how political power can obstruct spiritual renewal.

**Verse 24 — The cost of delay:** The work stopped for roughly fifteen years (from about 530 to 520 BCE). This gap would profoundly affect the community's morale and is the backdrop for the prophetic ministries of Haggai and Zechariah.

*— PNEUMA*
